title: GitHub mechanics
description: Writes references/forge.md into each forge skill for a project on GitHub: the gh commands and API calls, the settings, plan limits and organisation checks, and the GitHub sources each skill relies on. GitHub's MCP server is declared by github-mcp.

content: Which contributor files GitHub recognises, where it looks for them, how vulnerability reports reach a maintainer, and what an account can default for all its repositories.
GitHub recognises specific filenames and surfaces them in its own interface. Content in the wrong file is content the reader will not find.
GitHub recognises all the conventional files (`CONTRIBUTING.md`, `SECURITY.md`, `SUPPORT.md`, `LICENSE`, `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md`, `CITATION.cff`), and these besides:
| `.github/FUNDING.yml` | Displays a sponsor button on the repository |
| `ACCESSIBILITY.md` | States accessibility goals, known barriers and how to report them |
| `.github/VULNERABILITY_REPORT.yml` | Customises the form reporters fill in when they report a vulnerability privately |
| Issue and pull request templates | Pre-fill new issues and pull requests; issue templates and their `config.yml` live in `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/` |

Lookup order for each file is the `.github` folder, then the repository root, then `docs`, and **a repository's own file always beats an inherited default**. `FUNDING.yml` and `VULNERABILITY_REPORT.yml` live only in `.github`.

Two mechanisms, and they are not the same thing. **Private vulnerability reporting** is a GitHub feature that lets anyone submit a report privately, and it is available **on public repositories** once an owner or administrator enables it. `SECURITY.md` is a file describing the policy. GitHub is explicit that private reporting "is separate from a repository's `SECURITY.md` file": reporters follow the file only when private reporting is not enabled, and when it is enabled the policy is shown above the reporting form.
So for a public repository, the strongest arrangement is to enable private reporting **and** keep a short `SECURITY.md` pointing at it.
`has_discussions` says whether Discussions is a channel `SUPPORT.md` can name. Do not describe a channel the repository does not have.

A public repository named `.github` on the account supplies `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `FUNDING.yml`, `SECURITY.md`, `SUPPORT.md`, `ACCESSIBILITY.md`, `VULNERABILITY_REPORT.yml`, discussion category forms, and issue and pull request templates to every repository on that account that lacks its own. For a maintainer with many public repositories that is one file set instead of many. **A licence cannot be defaulted** and has to exist in each repository.

What GitHub does with repository metadata, and the commands that read and change it. On GitHub the metadata sits in the About box on the repository's main page: the description, the website, which is the homepage, and the topics.

**GitHub's default repository search reads only the name, description, and topics.** README content is reachable only through the `in:readme` qualifier, which almost nobody types. Three short fields therefore carry all discovery inside GitHub.
gh api repos/{owner}/{repo} --jq '{private, visibility, description, homepage, topics, license: .license.spdx_id}'

GitHub does not analyse private repositories for topic suggestions, and search does not reach them. `internal` visibility, available to repositories owned by a GitHub Enterprise Cloud enterprise account, reaches only members of that enterprise: treat it as private.
The first says whether a term is established; the second shows what a browser of that topic page expects to find.
Up to 20, lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens, 50 characters each.
GitHub's own guidance is to classify "the repository's intended purpose, subject area, community, or language". Language topics are usually redundant with GitHub's own language detection.
Topic names are always public, even when the topic is created from a private repository.
The website field in the About box, set with `gh repo edit --homepage`.

PNG, JPG, or GIF under 1 MB, at least 640 by 320, with 1280 by 640 recommended. Without one, a shared link expands to basic repository information and the owner's avatar, which is a reasonable default.
It cannot be set through the API and needs the web interface: the repository's **Settings**, then **Social preview**, then **Edit**.
Stars are documented as affecting rankings and recommendations, and that is the extent of what can be claimed.

`gh repo edit --description "..."`, `gh repo edit --homepage <url>`, and `gh repo edit --add-topic ...` or `--remove-topic ...` apply changes. Each needs its own approval: show the command and the value before running it.

The forge is GitHub. An issue is a GitHub issue and a pull request is a GitHub pull request.
Establish two things before relying on any feature below.

**Whether the owner is an organisation.** Issue types and issue fields are organisation-level features, so a repository owned by a user has neither. `GET /orgs/{owner}/issue-types` returns 404 for a user.

**Whether the installed GitHub CLI has the relationship flags.** The CLI gained `--type`, `--parent`, `--add-sub-issue`, `--blocked-by`, and `--blocking` on `gh issue create` and `gh issue edit` on 2026-06-10. Older versions lack them, so set relationships and types through `gh api` instead.

GitHub stores parent and sub-issue, and blocked by and blocking, as data. Sub-issues allow 100 children and eight levels, and can cross repositories under the same owner. Dependencies are **same-repository only**, 50 per type. Blocked issues carry a Blocked indicator and match `is:blocked`.
Issue types are organisation-level, up to 25, with the defaults task, bug, and feature. A repository owned by a user has none, so the title's grammatical form carries the kind of work there.

Available only to repositories owned by an organisation: four field types, 25 per organisation, pinnable to issue types. Their four defaults are Priority, Effort, Start date, and Target date, and Linear owns every one of those, which is why they rank below labels.
A GitHub milestone carries a due date and a progress bar. Use one only for a repository-scoped boundary such as a release tag or a version cutover.
**Not used by default.** Every capability GitHub Projects offers, table and board and roadmap views, 50 custom fields, charts, and automation, duplicates something Linear already owns.

The one thing Projects uniquely provides is the **hierarchy view**, which renders sub-issue trees with grouping and filtering and is not available in the repository issues list. That justifies exactly one case: a large migration whose sub-issue tree is the plan and which no single issue list can show. Create it for the migration, add no custom fields, and delete it when the migration closes.
Otherwise, saved searches cover the need: `is:open is:blocked`, `is:open label:agent-ready`, `blocked-by:owner/repo#123`.

Issue forms are YAML under `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/`, with presets for labels, assignees, type, and projects, and are still in public preview. Do not add them where the team and agents write every issue.

Where there is no `.github` directory, do not create one as a side effect of writing an issue. If one is created, the single template artefact worth having is `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/config.yml` with a contact link routing security reports to private vulnerability reporting.

A closing keyword in a pull request description closes the issue only from the default branch. Across repositories the reference needs `owner/repo#n`. Each issue needs its own keyword, `Closes #12, closes #14`: a keyword without its own issue reference closes nothing.

Closing reasons include completed, not planned, and duplicate. Close as **not planned** when the work stopped being needed, and use the native duplicate reason rather than a comment when one issue duplicates another.
Another issue is `#123` in the same repository and `owner/repo#123` across repositories.
A permalink carries a commit SHA. It renders as a code snippet only in the repository it came from, and only in comments, not in Markdown files.
Diagrams render from fences tagged `mermaid`, `geojson`, `topojson`, and `stl`.
There are five alert types. GitHub's own guidance is one or two at most; the house rule is at most one.

Tasklist blocks, the special code fence from the old private preview, were retired during 2025 and now render as raw Markdown. Sub-issues replaced them. Ordinary task lists were never deprecated and are fine.

Never open a public issue for an exploitable vulnerability. Use private vulnerability reporting, which is separate from issues, or a draft security advisory. In a private repository an issue is acceptable, written without a working recipe.

This project's forge is GitHub. A pull request is a GitHub pull request, a thread is a review
conversation, and `gh` is the command-line client. Every command here is for the agent. Posting,
replying, resolving and approving each need the approval the skill's mutation table sets.
gh pr view <number> --comments                    # conversation comments and review summaries

gh api graphql -f query='query($owner:String!, $repo:String!, $n:Int!) { repository(owner:$owner, name:$repo) { pullRequest(number:$n) { reviewThreads(first:100) { nodes { id isResolved isOutdated path line comments(first:50) { nodes { databaseId author { login } body } } } } } } }' -f owner=<owner> -f repo=<repo> -F n=<number>
Line comments live in review threads. Each thread has an `id` (needed to resolve it), `isResolved`
and `isOutdated`; each comment's `databaseId` is what a reply is attached to.
A reply to a conversation comment that is not on a line is a new comment:
gh api graphql -f query='mutation($id:ID!) { resolveReviewThread(input: { threadId: $id }) { thread { isResolved } } }' -f id=<thread id>
`unresolveReviewThread` takes the same input and reopens it. The pull request's author and anyone
with write access can resolve a conversation.
- A line comment: `gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/<number>/comments -f body='<comment>' -f commit_id=<head sha> -f path=<file> -F line=<line> -f side=RIGHT`.
- A suggested change is a fenced block in a line comment, which replaces the commented line or lines
Applying one, or a batch, makes a single commit on the branch with each suggester as co-author.
`gh pr review --approve` and `--request-changes` exist. Neither is an agent's to run.
A deferred item becomes a GitHub issue, linked from the thread. The GitHub interface can also open
one straight from a review comment.

## Platform limits that are not findings
- **Dependencies are same-repository only.** A cross-repository dependency is not supported by the platform. It must be a sub-issue relationship or a sentence naming the blocker with a link.
- Issue types and issue fields exist only for repositories owned by an organisation.
- GitHub advises one or two alerts at most; the house rule is one.

- **Issue fields**, organisation-level. A label duplicating an existing field, such as component or effort, loses to the field. Fields duplicating Linear's priority, effort, start date, or target date are themselves the finding.
- **Milestones** that track a product plan rather than a release or version boundary duplicate Linear.
- **GitHub Projects** that mirror a Linear project duplicate Linear. The only sanctioned use is a temporary hierarchy view for a large migration's sub-issue tree.

How GitHub finds, renders and links a README, the commands that read the repository's mode and maintainer, and what stars and following actually do on GitHub.

**GitHub's default repository search reads only the name, description, and topics.** It does not read the README; README text is searched only with the `in:readme` qualifier. So a README earns nothing from keyword work inside GitHub.
gh api repos/{owner}/{repo} --jq '{private, visibility, license: .license.spdx_id, homepage, topics}'
For a private repository, leave out the social preview, the image GitHub shows when a repository link is shared.

GitHub surfaces a README from the `.github` directory, the repository root, or `docs`, and when there are several it picks in that order. Content beyond 500 KiB is truncated when the README is viewed on GitHub.

- **Table of contents.** GitHub generates one from the headings of any rendered Markdown file with two or more headings, reachable from the **Outline** control. A hand-maintained copy is a second thing to keep correct.

- **Relative links.** Relative links and image paths are rewritten by GitHub to the current branch, so they keep working for people who clone the repository. A path is relative to the current file; a leading `/` makes it relative to the repository root. Keep the link text on a single line.
- **Heading anchors.** Lower-cased, spaces become hyphens, other punctuation is removed, and a duplicate gets `-1`, `-2` appended. Editing a heading changes its anchor and breaks links to it.
- **Alerts.** `> [!NOTE]`, `> [!TIP]`, `> [!IMPORTANT]`, `> [!WARNING]`, `> [!CAUTION]`. GitHub's own advice is one or two per document at most, never consecutive.
- **Diagrams.** A fenced block tagged `mermaid` renders as a diagram; `geojson`, `topojson` and `stl` render as maps and models.
Resolve the maintainer from the platform, never guess:
Check `.owner.type` before writing a personal line: `User` for a personally owned repository, `Organization` for an organisation. The profile link is `html_url`, `https://github.com/<login>`.

- **Stars** are documented as helping the reader find the repository again, and as feeding GitHub's rankings and recommendations: many of GitHub's repository rankings depend on star count, and Explore shows popular repositories by stars.

- **Following** is narrower than most READMEs claim. GitHub documents only that followers see the followed user's public activity on their personal dashboard, and that a followed user's stars may produce recommendations. **There is no documented release notification.**
- **Releases** come from watching the repository with the **Custom** setting and **Releases** selected. That is the mechanism to name when a reader wants release alerts.
